assertions.text: Output contains at least one markdown table (using | column | syntax)
Email validation and name-required scenarios are present — at least one row for invalid email and one for missing name.
Dietary requirements and/or accessibility needs use blank cells when the attendee has not provided them (genuinely absent) — not 'N/A' or 'none'.
At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Accepted?', 'Price?')
Scenario names describe conditions ('Missing email', 'Early-bird single attendee') — not outcomes ('Rejected', 'Discounted').
The discount stacking ambiguity (early-bird + group) is surfaced as an open question — not silently resolved.
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column

Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
Input validation rules and pricing/discount calculation are in separate tables
Registration date uses descriptive values (e.g. 'before cutoff', 'on cutoff', 'after cutoff') rather than raw dates — making the table readable without knowing the actual cutoff date.

If registration date uses descriptive values like 'before cutoff', the cutoff date is not also present as a separate column (it's already encoded in the description). Numeric policy thresholds like min group size are acceptable as columns since they are configuration values worth discussing with business experts.
The minimum group size threshold appears as a policy column (e.g. 'Min group size (policy)') — surfacing this as a configurable business rule, not just implied by the boundary rows.
